title: Bleached Reefs and the Search for Resilience
context:
Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to about a quarter of all marine species. The builders of a reef are corals, which are animals, not plants. Each is a colony of tiny polyps whose tissues contain microscopic algae. The two live in partnership: the algae use sunlight to make sugars, supplying the coral with most of its energy, while the coral provides shelter and the chemicals the algae need. The arrangement is highly efficient, but it is also delicate. Their loss would therefore affect fisheries and coastal communities as well as divers and scientists.

Trouble begins when the water stays about one degree Celsius above the normal summer maximum for several weeks. Under heat stress, the algae start to produce harmful compounds, and the coral responds by expelling them. Without the algae, the coral's transparent tissue reveals the white skeleton beneath, hence the term bleaching. A bleached coral is not necessarily dead. If temperatures fall within a few weeks, the algae can return and the colony recovers. If the heat continues, however, the coral starves. The first worldwide bleaching event was recorded in 1998, and since then such events have become more frequent. On the Great Barrier Reef, the average gap between severe episodes has shrunk from decades to roughly six years, and in 2016 and 2017 the reef was struck twice in succession, leaving too little time for recovery.

Yet the damage has not been uniform. Fast-growing branching corals, which provide hiding places for fish, are among the most vulnerable, whereas slow-growing boulder-shaped species often survive. Some reefs have even adapted to extraordinary conditions: those in the Persian Gulf endure summer temperatures that would kill most corals elsewhere. These exceptions have encouraged scientists to ask whether resilience can be encouraged, or even engineered.

Several approaches are being tested. In selective breeding, researchers cross the most heat-tolerant colonies and raise their offspring in tanks, hoping to produce tougher stock. Others try exposing young corals to mild stress so that they become accustomed to it, or replacing their algae with heat-tolerant varieties. In coral gardening, fragments are grown in underwater nurseries and then attached to damaged reefs. These projects have produced encouraging results on a small scale, but a nursery that grows thousands of fragments a year is dwarfed by a reef system stretching over two thousand kilometres. Critics add that favouring a few tolerant strains may reduce genetic diversity, leaving reefs vulnerable to other threats.

Local conditions also matter. Reefs that suffer from polluted run-off or from overfishing recover more slowly than those that do not. In particular, parrotfish and other grazing species keep seaweed under control, and when they are caught in excess, seaweed can smother the young corals trying to re-establish themselves. Protecting reefs from these local pressures therefore buys valuable time, and in several regions it has measurably improved survival rates after bleaching.

Time, though, is what the technology cannot ultimately provide. Climate models suggest that at 1.5 degrees of global warming, between seventy and ninety per cent of warm-water reefs would be lost, and at two degrees virtually all of them. Interventions such as breeding and gardening are best seen as emergency measures that give reefs a chance to survive until emissions fall. They are worth pursuing, but they are not a substitute for the harder task of cutting those emissions.
